contract_plain_english: For one coordinate of a standard Gaussian vector and a positive threshold t, squaring turns the tail event into the absolute Gaussian tail at √t. The Gaussian exponent therefore becomes exp(−t/2), so the book describes the square as having an exponential-type tail, heavier than a sub-gaussian one. This is an exponential-scale description: Proposition 2.1.2 supplies a polynomial Mills-ratio factor, and the Section 2.7 footnote explicitly says such a factor was suppressed. [PDF page 20; printed page 31; anchor: Section 2.7 opening paragraph, display, following sentence, and footnote 6; PDF page 2; printed page 13; anchor: Proposition 2.1.2]

source_evidence.anchor: Section 2.7 opening paragraph beginning “Consider a standard normal random vector”
source_evidence.observation: The source introduces g = (g₁, …, g_N) ∈ ℝ^N as a standard normal random vector and states that its coordinates gᵢ are independent N(0,1) random variables.
The displayed calculation is P{gᵢ² > t} = P{|g| > √t} ∼ exp(−(√t)²/2) = exp(−t/2).

source_evidence.anchor: Sentence immediately following the Section 2.7 opening display
source_evidence.observation: The source concludes that the tails of gᵢ² are like those of the exponential distribution and are strictly heavier than sub-gaussian tails.

source_evidence.anchor: Footnote 6 attached to the Section 2.7 opening display
source_evidence.observation: The source says that it ignored a pre-factor 1/t because this does not have much effect on the exponent.
For a scalar g ∼ N(0,1) and every u > 0, the source gives (1/u − 1/u³)(1/√(2π))exp(−u²/2) ≤ P{g ≥ u} ≤ (1/u)(1/√(2π))exp(−u²/2).
For u ≥ 1, the source records the simpler upper bound P{g ≥ u} ≤ (1/√(2π))exp(−u²/2).

definitions_and_conventions: A standard normal random vector in this passage means a vector whose coordinates are independent N(0,1) random variables. [PDF page 20; printed page 31; anchor: Section 2.7 opening paragraph]
The equality of events underlying the first probability identity is gᵢ² > t if and only if |gᵢ| > √t for t > 0. [PDF page 20; printed page 31; anchor: Section 2.7 opening display]

The symbol ∼ in the opening display is an informal exponential-scale comparison, not an assertion that the ratio of the two displayed quantities tends to one, because the accompanying footnote explicitly discards a polynomial pre-factor. hypotheses: Each coordinate gᵢ has distribution N(0,1), and the coordinates are independent. [PDF page 20; printed page 31; anchor: Section 2.7 opening paragraph]
implicit_context: The probability is taken with respect to the law of the standard normal vector introduced immediately before the display. [PDF page 20; printed page 31; anchor: Section 2.7 opening paragraph and display]

Only the one-coordinate marginal law is needed for this tail calculation; coordinate independence belongs to the surrounding vector context. [PDF page 20; printed page 31; anchor: Section 2.7 opening paragraph and display]

The scalar g in P{|g| > √t} is not the vector g under the Euclidean norm; it denotes a one-dimensional standard normal representative of the coordinate law. [PDF page 20; printed page 31; anchor: opening paragraph and opening display]

details: Squaring converts a threshold t for gᵢ² into the threshold √t for the absolute value of a scalar standard normal coordinate. [PDF page 20; printed page 31; anchor: Section 2.7 opening display]
Substituting u = √t into the Gaussian exponential exp(−u²/2) produces exp(−t/2). [PDF page 20; printed page 31; anchor: Section 2.7 opening display]
Thus the logarithmic or exponential rate in t is −1/2. [PDF page 20; printed page 31; anchor: Section 2.7 opening display and footnote 6]
Proposition 2.1.2 shows that a Gaussian tail also carries a reciprocal-threshold factor. [PDF page 2; printed page 13; anchor: Proposition 2.1.2]

After setting u = √t and accounting for the two symmetric tails, the corresponding polynomial scale is t^(−1/2), up to lower-order correction and an absolute constant; this is a consequence of the cited proposition rather than the literal pre-factor stated in footnote 6.
